claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
Mechanical loading under demanding service conditions can induce local phase separation or stress-driven precipitation.
Loading-induced precipitates or phase-separated regions form preferentially at grain boundaries or within localized shear bands.
The resulting microstructural heterogeneities create weak sites for crack initiation.
Reduced temperatures reduce the alloy's ductility.
An inert testing atmosphere prevents oxidation from influencing the experiment.
Stress-induced precipitates or phase-separated regions reduce local toughness.
High mechanical stress increases the driving force for local compositional fluctuations.
Stress-enhanced compositional fluctuations lead to nucleation of a second, brittle phase.
Formation of the second phase undermines the homogeneous deformation mechanisms of the single-phase alloy.
Disruption of homogeneous deformation reduces toughness and promotes crack initiation and propagation.
Samples loaded at high strain rates and low temperatures will have lower strain-to-failure than the ambient-temperature, moderate-rate baseline.
Samples loaded under the demanding conditions will exhibit brittle-fracture evidence.
Phase separation or precipitate formation will be spatially correlated with reduced toughness.
At moderate loading rates and ambient temperature, the baseline alloy has high toughness and retains microstructural homogeneity.
High strain rates and sub-ambient or cryogenic temperatures challenge the stability of the homogeneous phase and make microstructural transformations more likely.
The critical strain rate or temperature for transformation depends on alloy composition and processing history.
Residual stresses from processing may influence the onset of brittleness.
Control and demanding-condition specimens will be prepared from the same alloy batch and compared mechanically and microstructurally.
The hypothesis is falsified if demanding-condition samples show neither a significant toughness reduction nor identifiable phase separation or precipitation.

contradictions.description: The design places synchrotron XRD after mechanical testing and describes analysis on fracture surfaces, whereas the measurements describe in-situ XRD monitoring microstructural evolution in real time during loading.
